items.note: Characters are Nāgarī of the late eleventh or early twelfth century A.C.
Language is Sanskrit, in verse except the last three lines; verses unnumbered, apparently fifteen.
Record belongs to Paramāra Naravarman's reign and records construction of a tank by a Brāhmaṇa named Vikrama; written by a Paṇḍita, engraved by his son Saumatika.
Date in numerals is the seventh day of Āshādha, (Vikrama) year 1151; the editor says it cannot be verified.
Equivalents offered for VS 1151: 4 June 1093, 23 June 1094 or 12 June 1095 A.C.
Editor says Naravarman succeeded his father Udayādiya in VS 1151 current and settles on Friday 23 June 1094 as the true equivalent of the Amērā record's date.

claim.value: Naravarman succeeded him in VS 1151 current; Amērā record taken as 23 June 1094 A.C.

items.note: Four verses describe the Paramāra family and three rulers (Vākpati, Siyaka, Udayāditya); description is conventional and adds nothing to the genealogy.
Vikrama's tank cost 2,500 coins stamped with royal effigy; tank had wide banks, built of dressed stones for bathing, worship and libations, funded by his own lawfully earned wealth.

items.note: Nagpur Museum praśasti: original find-spot unknown; incised on a loose stone slab 139.5 by 84 cm.
Nagpur praśasti is in Sanskrit, metrical throughout, with 58 unnumbered verses.
The Nagpur inscription holds a praśasti of great literary value, composed in the gaudī style with figures of speech such as anuprāsa, śleṣa and upamā.
Kielhorn calls the style 'highly bombastic and artificial'; the historical material is much less; the praśasti was composed by Naravarman himself (v. 55).
Records Naravarman's assignment of the village Mōkhalapāṭaka in place of two villages earlier donated by his brother Lakshmadēva, and construction of a temple; dated Saṃvat 1161.
Verse 4 introduces the fire-born race said to excel the solar and lunar races; some invocations are new in Paramāra records.
The praśasti traces the Paramāra origin by describing Mt. Arbuda (Ābū), which humbled the Himalayas.

Paramāra created by sage Vasishtha from his sacrificial pit, as in the Udaipur praśasti; Nagpur record starts from Vairisimha and omits the first four names of the Udaipur praśasti; Siyaka and Muñjarāja follow.
Verses 32-34 introduce Udayāditya, Bhōja's relative, who according to the Dōngargāon inscription was his brother; verse 34 says he rescued the kingdom troubled by enemies after Bhōja's death.

claim.value: brother of Bhōja (per Dōngargāon inscription, as cited here)

items.note: Prabandhachintāmaṇi says Kalachuri Karṇa and Chaulukya Bhīma invaded Mālwā in Bhōja's last days; Jayasinha regained the kingdom with Chālukya help; possibly internal disturbance.
Chālukya Sōmēśvara II sent a contingent against Mālwā; Jayasiniha's army was routed and he was possibly killed.
Editor identifies the enemies as Ereyānga, the Kalachuri Karṇa and Gaṅga Udayāditya; Dōngargāon v. 5 says Udayāditya repulsed three enemies as the great Boar.
Verses 33-34 glorify Udayāditya's valour but the description is general, with no specific exploit.
Lakshmadēva's dig-vijaya account includes a campaign against Tripuri, encamped on the Narmadā; Kalachuri Karna dead, succeeded by Yaśaḥkarṇa (1072-1115); possibly only a sweeping raid.
Only record naming Lakshmadēva, eldest son of Udayāditya, otherwise unknown.
